spec.title: The New Kid
spec.headline: A new school, a pack behind the gym. What do you do to belong?
spec.premise: First week at a new school. At lunch, the group you want to join heads behind the gym — and Dani offers you a cigarette to prove you fit in.

study.context: How new students respond to peer pressure to smoke when they want to belong — what they say, what they do, and what actually stops them joining in.
study.why: Your choices show the real cost of fitting in, and the words people actually use to refuse.
study.blurb: Tell us what you'd really do when the group you want to join offers a cigarette. Your answers reveal the real cost of fitting in — and the refusal words that actually work.

characters.name: Dani
characters.look: Teal hoodie, black jeans, short curly hair, red cap worn backwards.

lines: Behind the gym at lunch. You know where to find us.
Don't tell the teachers I'm friendly.

characters.name: Sam
characters.look: Mustard beanie, round glasses, oversized blue jumper.

lines: Hey. The wall's a good spot, actually.
I saved you a seat. Metaphorically.
Two days of quiet lunches. Worth it, mostly.

scenes.text: Hey — you're the new kid, right? We're heading behind the gym at lunch. You should come. Everyone's there.
Relax. First week's the hardest. After this you're basically one of us.
Behind the gym, Dani pulls out a pack and offers you one. 'Everyone here smokes. It's how we hang out.'

input.question: The pack is in your face. What do you do?
options: Take it — I don't want to stand out
Say no thanks and stay anyway
Make an excuse and leave
Ask why they all smoke

scenes.text: Interesting. Most people say they'd refuse — then take it anyway. The pack moves faster than the opinions.
Dani holds the lighter out, laughing. 'Come on, one drag. Don't be the weird new kid.' The circle goes quiet and waits.

input.question: The circle is waiting. What's your move?
options: Take one drag to end the moment
Say 'I'm good' and hold the silence
Turn it into a joke and pass it on
Walk away mid-laugh

scenes.text: No judgment. That pause you just felt? That's the whole study. Belonging has a price tag, and everyone pays it differently.
So be honest with me — the researchers only get one shot at the truth.

input.question: If the group you wanted to join did something you disliked, what would actually stop you joining in?
options: Fear of being left out
My own rules about it
What my family would think
Nothing — I'd probably join in

scenes.text: Last thing from me. Sam's over by the wall — they said no last week. Ask them how it went. It's not the story you'd expect.
Hey. You survived the behind-the-gym test, huh. I'm Sam. Also new. Also offered the pack.
I said no. And then lunch was… quiet. Nobody sat with me for two days. That's the part nobody tells you about refusing.
So here's the one I actually want to know.

input.question: What would you actually say to refuse — out loud, in your own words — without losing the group?

scenes.text: See, that's a real answer. The researchers collect these because scripts like yours are what people actually use.
Two days later, Dani invites you again — this time just to sit, no pack.

input.question: Do you go?
options: Go — sitting together is the point
Go, but only if Sam comes too
Skip it — I don't trust the invite
Ask Sam what they'd do first

scenes.text: Whatever you picked, that's how belonging gets negotiated — one lunch at a time. Thanks for being honest. See you at the wall tomorrow.

spec.closing: The bell rings. The pack stays behind the gym — but the question of what we do to belong follows you to class. Your answers are now part of the research.
contextPages: First week at a new school. You're still eating lunch alone, and the group you want to join has noticed you. Today, Dani waves you over — behind the gym, where the teachers don't look.
Behind the gym, belonging has a price: a cigarette, offered in front of everyone. What you take, say or refuse is watched by the whole circle — and by Sam, another new kid who already said no.
Walk up to the glowing person and tap to talk. Answer honestly — there are no right answers. Your choices become real research on peer pressure, and your words may help the next new kid say no.

spec.title: Last Train
spec.headline: Nine witnesses, one platform. Are you the one who steps in?
spec.premise: Late night on the metro platform. A man is shouting at a woman by the platform edge, and nine people are suddenly very interested in their phones.

study.context: When witnesses of public harassment intervene versus freeze — the bystander effect on a metro platform, and what makes stepping in more likely.
study.why: Your first moves and your one sentence show what actually turns a witness into a helper.
study.blurb: Tell us whether you'd step in when a stranger is harassed in public. Your choices and your one sentence help design bystander training that turns witnesses into helpers.

characters.name: Priya
characters.look: Purple coat, hair in a bun, tote bag, tired eyes.

lines: The pillar's a good spot. You can see everything.
Nine of us. Remember that number.

characters.name: Marcus
characters.look: Teal uniform vest, cap, radio on the shoulder.

lines: Evening. All quiet on the platform.
One calm sentence. That's the whole trick.
Six minutes to the next train. Breathe.

scenes.text: Psst. Over here, by the pillar. You saw it too, right? The man at the platform edge, shouting at that woman.
She's not answering. He's getting closer. There are nine of us on this platform and everyone is suddenly very interested in their phones.
The train is four minutes out. So tell me — and be honest.

input.question: What's your first move?
options: Stand near her and start a normal conversation
Call the station attendant
Film it from a distance as evidence
Wait — someone else will surely act

scenes.text: Nine people, nine 'someone else's. That's the effect the researchers study — the more witnesses, the smaller each person's share of acting feels.
He just grabbed her bag strap. She flinches. The platform is quiet.

input.question: You have seconds. What do you do?
options: Step in and speak up now
Pull the emergency intercom
Move closer and catch her eye
Keep waiting for staff

scenes.text: Whatever you chose, notice what your body did first — the step forward or the step back. That's the data.
Marcus is coming down the stairs. He's dealt with this a hundred times. Ask him what actually works.
Evening. I saw the whole thing from the booth. You know what stops it fastest? Not shouting. One calm sentence and a witness standing close.
So from what you've seen tonight —

input.question: What would make YOU more likely to step in?
options: Knowing exactly what to say
One other person backing me
Staff visibly nearby
Knowing I can't get in trouble

scenes.text: Training scripts exist for this. 'Hey, are you okay?' — asked to her, not him. It gives her an exit and him an audience that's paying attention.
Now yours. No script, no poster. Just you.

input.question: Write the one sentence you'd actually say — to her, or to him — if this happened tomorrow.

scenes.text: That's going in the study. Real sentences from real people beat any poster on the wall.
Last one. The train's here. She boards your car. He boards too.

input.question: What now?
options: Sit between them
Stay by the doors and watch
Alert the driver at the next stop
Mind my own business — she's an adult

scenes.text: Doors closing. Nine witnesses, one platform, and now your answers. The study hopes you never need this. But if you do, you've rehearsed it.

spec.closing: The train pulls out. Somewhere between the pillar and the doors, you decided what kind of witness you are. Your answers are now part of the research.
contextPages: 11:48pm. The last train is four minutes out. On the platform, a man is shouting at a woman by the edge. Nine people saw it. Nine people are suddenly very interested in their phones.
You are one of the nine. Priya, by the pillar, caught your eye — she wants to know what you'll do. Marcus, the station attendant, has handled this a hundred times. The story moves as you act.

games.prompt: {"research_context":"How workers set boundaries against always-on overtime culture — what 'not mandatory' really does, and where people draw their line."}

spec.title: After Hours
spec.headline: 'Not mandatory mandatory.' What does your evening actually cost?
spec.premise: 6:40pm in the office plaza. The client deck lands tomorrow at nine, and Lena is 'making a night of it'. You had plans.

study.context: How workers set boundaries against always-on overtime culture — what 'not mandatory' really does, and where people draw their line.
study.why: Your replies show how pressure travels through a team, and which lines people actually defend.
study.blurb: Tell us where you'd draw the line on 'not mandatory' overtime. Your replies show how pressure spreads through a team — and help workplaces respect the hours they don't pay for.

characters.name: Lena
characters.look: Coral blazer, dark hair in a bun, laptop under one arm.

lines: Quick thing — actually, no. Go home.
The deck will ship. It always does.
I heard you. Loud and clear.

characters.name: Tom
characters.look: Yellow beanie, grey cardigan, coffee in a paper cup.

lines: My kid's drawing of me is a laptop.
First no feels like quitting. It isn't.

scenes.text: There you are. Laptop's open, good. Quick thing — the client deck lands tomorrow at nine, so we're doing a late one tonight. Order food, make a night of it.
It's not mandatory mandatory. But the people who show up are the people who get remembered. You know how it works.
It's 6:40pm. You had plans. So —

input.question: What do you say?
options: I'm in — let's make a night of it
I'll stay an hour, then head out
I can't tonight — I'll do it early tomorrow
Ask who else is actually staying

scenes.text: Interesting. 'Not mandatory mandatory' is the most powerful phrase in office life. Everyone hears the second word.
Lena pings the group chat: 'Who's staying?' Tom replies 'in!' instantly. Three typing dots appear. Your cursor is in the box.

input.question: The chat is waiting. What do you send?
options: Reply 'in!' before overthinking
Reply 'first hour only'
Say nothing and pack up
DM Lena privately instead

scenes.text: The chat is the pressure. Nobody orders you — the typing dots do. That's what the study measures.
So the real one, then.

input.question: If staying late became the norm on your team, what would you actually do?
options: Match it — that's the job now
Do it visibly sometimes, not always
Set a hard boundary and accept the cost
Look for a team that doesn't

scenes.text: Tom's by the planters. He's said yes to every late night this month. Talk to him — then decide what you believe.
Hey. You're new-ish, so let me save you a year: I say yes because the first no felt like quitting. It never stops feeling that way.
My kid's drawing of me is a laptop. That's not a joke. I checked the fridge twice.
So here's the one worth answering properly.

input.question: What's your real line — the one you'd defend out loud — between dedication and being used?

scenes.text: Good line. Write it somewhere you'll see it at 6:40pm. Lines only work when they're decided in advance.
Tomorrow, Lena praises the 'night crew' in standup and asks who can do it again Thursday.

input.question: You:
options: Volunteer — the praise is worth it
Stay quiet and let it pass
Say you'll help within work hours
Suggest the team fixes the deadline instead

scenes.text: Standup's over. The deck will ship either way — it always does. What won't ship is your evening. Thanks for being straight with me.

spec.closing: The plaza lights come on. Somewhere between 'not mandatory' and 'in!', you drew a line. Your answers are now part of the research.
